channel.title: Lexoral — Blog
channel.description: Legal transcription in Canada and the United States: guides, and a regular watch on transcription and justice.

item.title: Record watch: transcription and justice in Canada and the U.S. — week of October 19, 2026
item.description: California drops machine translation at court counters; in Congress, the bill to study automatic transcription in courts gains a Senate co-sponsor.

item.title: Record watch: transcription and justice in Canada and the U.S. — week of October 12, 2026
item.description: Oklahoma records its courtrooms but keeps the certified reporter; in California, court interpreters walk out over pay and remote interpreting.

item.title: Record watch: transcription and justice in Canada and the U.S. — mid-October 2026
item.description: The Texas Supreme Court hears the AI transcript case, Oklahoma weighs courtroom recording, and Ottawa wants federal AI to respect both official languages.

item.title: Record watch: transcription and justice in Canada and the U.S. — early October 2026
item.description: NCSC guidance on AI-assisted transcription in courts, and an Ontario Court of Appeal ruling on French when the province’s lawyers are on the other side.

item.title: Record watch: transcription and justice in Canada and the U.S. — late September 2026
item.description: An AI-assisted transcript before the Texas Supreme Court, a new California court-reporting law, and an Acadian courthouse at the Supreme Court of Canada.

item.title: What a legal transcript is for — and who actually reads it
item.description: A transcript is not a set of notes: it is the record. Who reads it (appeal courts, counsel, judges, witnesses), how it is cited, and why accuracy matters.

item.title: Court reporter, transcriptionist, interpreter: who does what
item.description: Three jobs that get confused. In Quebec, Ontario and the U.S.: who takes the record, who transcribes it, who interprets, and what each one produces.

item.title: Deposing a Canadian witness for a U.S. case
item.description: Canada is not a party to the Hague Evidence Convention. Willing witnesses, letters rogatory, and what to plan for when the witness speaks French.

item.title: Record watch: transcription and justice in Canada and the U.S. — September 2026
item.description: California allows recording when no court reporter is available, North Dakota moves to audio, AI next, and language is back before Quebec’s Superior Court.
